source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC10066463 (JAMA Netw Open 2023;6(3):e236185; the corrected version), read in full in the built-in browser: key points, abstract, introduction, methods, results, Tables 1-4, discussion, limitations, conclusions, author information (contributions, conflict-of-interest disclosures, funding, role of funder) and the reference list (for the years of the included studies). Figure checked on screen; its values are printed in it. Correction notice PMC10170333 read: it corrects 95% CIs in the Figure and Supplement only. OSF registration doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G (registry record, osf.io/pf95g) read in full for the card check only, after step 1; the paper's reference 11 URL (osf.io/tnhd3) opened to confirm what it shows. Supplement 1 (eAppendix, eTables 1-3, eFigures 1-4) not read.

claims.note: Every Zhao 2023 number in the statement and magnitude matches Tables 2 and 4. Fully adjusted, all studies: 25 to <45 g a day 1.05 (0.96-1.14), 45 to <65 g 1.19 (1.07-1.32), 65 g or more 1.35 (1.23-1.47). Men: 1.01 (0.93-1.10), 1.15 (1.03-1.28), 1.34 (1.23-1.47). Women: 1.21 (1.08-1.36), 1.34 (1.11-1.63), 1.61 (1.44-1.80). The reference group is described correctly: the fully adjusted estimates come from a meta-regression with study-level covariates for abstainer biases, while the table labels the reference 'lifetime nondrinker'. 'Close to no difference' at 25 to 44 g is a fairer reading of 1.05 (0.96-1.14) than the authors' own 'increased risk ... for drinkers who drank 25 g or more' (Discussion, 1st paragraph). 'Higher in women than in men' rests on a sex interaction tested across all levels (P = .001), not at 25 to 44 g alone. Women's estimates at 45 g or more rest on few studies (17 studies, 19 estimates; 11 studies, 12 estimates). The 45 g threshold also holds in both age strata of cohorts (younger: 1.24 at 45 to <65 g; older: 1.15) and with partial adjustment (1.11, 1.03-1.21). Arithmetic: 45 g a day x 7 = 315 g a week (correct).

anchors.locator: Table 2 (reference group = lifetime nondrinker, fully adjusted column); Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers From Meta-analysis of Pooled Studies, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results
anchors.extracted: 107 studies, 724 estimates. Fully adjusted (between-study variation, abstainer biases, median age, sex, country, publication year, follow-up years, drinking pattern, and study-level control for heart problems, social status, race, diet, exercise, BMI and smoking): 25 to <45 g a day RR 1.05 (0.96-1.14), P = .28, 80 studies/146 estimates; 45 to <65 g 1.19 (1.07-1.32), 52/76; 65 g or more 1.35 (1.23-1.47), 45/83. Weighted with between-study variation only: 0.97 (0.92-1.02), 1.11 (1.03-1.21), 1.24 (1.16-1.32). Unweighted: 1.02, 1.07 (0.99-1.16), 1.35 (1.26-1.46).

anchors.locator: Table 4; Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers by Sex, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Fully adjusted, against lifetime nondrinkers of the same sex. Men: 25 to <45 g 1.01 (0.93-1.10; 54 studies/70 estimates), 45 to <65 g 1.15 (1.03-1.28; 37/41), 65 g or more 1.34 (1.23-1.47; 36/52). Women: 1.21 (1.08-1.36; 37/42), 1.34 (1.11-1.63; 17/19), 1.61 (1.44-1.80; 11/12). All women who drank against women lifetime nondrinkers: 1.22 (1.02-1.46). Women's RRs were higher across all levels (P for interaction = .001).

anchors.locator: Table 3; Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk on the Basis of Median Age of Study Cohorts at Baseline, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Fully adjusted by cohort median age at enrollment. Under 56 years: 25 to <45 g 1.06 (0.96-1.16), 45 to <65 g 1.24 (1.10-1.40), 65 g or more 1.38 (1.23-1.55). 56 years or over: 1.04 (0.95-1.14), 1.15 (1.02-1.30), 1.32 (1.18-1.47). Age interaction P = .02. Cohorts recruited at 50 or younger and followed to 60 had higher RRs in all drinking groups, but those values are only in eTable 3 (supplement, not read).

The authors summarize the fully adjusted models as showing increased risk from 25 g a day and significantly increased risk from 45 g a day. The 25 to <45 g estimate itself (1.05, 0.96-1.14) is compatible with no difference.

Intake was imperfectly measured and in many studies assessed only once. Self-reported intake is under-reported in most epidemiological studies. In several studies most self-reported lifetime abstainers are in fact former drinkers. In that case the risks relative to presumed lifetime abstainers are underestimated.

claims.note: These Zhao 2023 numbers match: 107 cohorts; 4,838,825 people; 425,564 deaths; unweighted low volume 0.85 (0.81-0.88); fully adjusted 0.93 (0.85-1.01), occasional 0.96 (0.86-1.06), former 1.26 (1.12-1.42); against occasional drinkers, fully adjusted, low volume 0.97 (0.85-1.11) and abstainers 1.04 (0.94-1.16); I2 above 85.87%. The statement's 107-cohort figure 0.86 (0.83-0.88) is also printed in Zhao 2023: it is the partially adjusted column of Table 2 (weighted, between-study variation; 99 studies, 306 estimates), the like-for-like counterpart of Stockwell 2016's 0.86 (0.83-0.90). The magnitude gives it under Stockwell et al. 2024. P for the fully adjusted 0.93 is .07 in the abstract and Results text but .08 in Table 2 and the Figure. 'Published 1981 to 2021': the search covered January 1980 to July 2021. The earliest included studies are from 1981 (refs 79, 110 and 122), and two included studies are in 2022 print issues (refs 30, 31). '1981 to 2021' is right if 'published' means first appearance. 'Mostly North America, Europe and Australia' is right: 94 of 108 country entries in Table 1 ('North and Central America' includes Cuba). Minor range point: the statement gives former drinkers 'relative risks 1.22 to 1.38' in the main models. Zhao's partially adjusted model gives 1.17 (1.08-1.26), the counterpart of Stockwell 2016's 1.22. If that model counts, the range is 1.17 to 1.38. Direction unchanged. Conversions recomputed: 1.3 g a day = 9.1 g a week, about one 10-g drink (the paper's own '<9.1 g per week'). 25 g a day is 2.5 drinks of 10 g, or about 2 Canadian standard drinks of 13.45 g as the Key Points say. 'About two drinks a day' follows the sources' own descriptions but understates slightly for 10-g drinks. A qualification the claim does not state (Figure): removing almost any single study-level covariate from the full model makes the low-volume estimate significant (0.90 to 0.92, P = .005 to .04). So the non-significance of 0.93 depends on including the whole covariate set. 'Insufficient to say' and 'contested' remain the right wording.

anchors.extracted: PubMed and Web of Science, any language, January 1980 to July 2021. The 87 studies of Stockwell et al. 2016 plus 20 new give 107 cohort studies, 724 risk estimates, 4,838,825 participants and 425,564 deaths. Reference groups: 21 studies (220 estimates) strictly lifetime abstainers; 50 (265) with both former and occasional drinkers; 28 (177) former only; 8 (62) occasional only. Earliest included studies 1981 (three); latest online in 2021, two in 2022 print issues.

North and Central America 41 studies (37.96%), Europe and Australia 53 (49.07%), Asia 14 (12.96%); 108 entries for 107 studies. Unweighted mean RR for any drinking by reference-group type: neither bias 1.19 (1.12-1.25), both biases 0.98 (0.92-1.04), former only 1.05 (0.98-1.12), occasional only 1.01 (0.89-1.13).

anchors.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Key Points › Findings
anchors.extracted: Categories: former drinkers (now abstaining), occasional (under 9.1 g a week), low volume (1.3-24.0 g a day in the text; 1.30 to <25 in the tables), medium 25-44, high 45-64, highest 65 or more g a day. Inverse-variance weights; mixed models with a random study effect. Analyses repeated with occasional drinkers as the reference. Key Points: under 25 g a day is about 2 Canadian standard drinks.

anchors.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph; author list and Author Contributions
anchors.extracted: This is an update of Stockwell et al. 2016 by an overlapping team (Zhao, Stockwell, Naimi in both). The same 87 studies are reused, with 20 new ones added.

Intake often measured once; self-report under-reported. Self-reported lifetime abstainers may mostly be former drinkers in several studies. Simply removing former drinkers may favour drinkers. Few studies in some strata. Binge drinking could not be examined. Findings concern net all-cause mortality.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed. The editors' count reproduces from the reference lists. Of the earlier 87 studies (refs 45-131), 14 are bias-free (refs 45-58), 41 have both biases, 24 former only and 8 occasional only. Of the 20 new studies (refs 13-32): 7 bias-free, 9 both, 4 former only. Totals 21, 50, 28 and 8.

Confirmed. Values can be added from the Figure (printed; CIs as corrected). Removing one covariate at a time from the full model (0.93, 0.85-1.01, P = .08) mostly gives 0.90 to 0.92 with P < .05. Examples: smoking 0.91 (0.84-0.99), drinking pattern 0.91 (0.85-0.98), former-drinker bias 0.90 (0.84-0.98), median age 0.91 (0.84-0.99), follow-up 0.91 (0.86-0.98). Removing diet, exercise, BMI or country leaves 0.93 to 0.94, not significant. All covariates removed: 0.86 (0.83-0.88).
Confirmed: notice PMC10170333 read; it lists only the Figure and Supplement CIs.

Confirmed against the registration (osf.io/pf95g, read in full): registered 3 November 2021; five hypotheses; English-language inclusion criterion; search from 1 July 2016 to 30 June 2021 with 31 new studies; the planned analyses as listed; no analyses yet run for the new plan; patterns for hypotheses 1-3 already known.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed: the four sex lists hold 110 entries and 105 distinct studies. Refs 13, 21, 26, 29 and 84 appear twice; refs 60 and 131 appear in none (recounted).

Confirmed: osf.io/tnhd3 opens Tim Stockwell's OSF user profile, which links to the project. The registration (3 November 2021) says no analyses for the new plan had been run, while the paper dates analysis from September 2021.

Confirmed, with a nuance. The registration's own search-strategy paragraph also says articles were identified 'regardless of language'. English is required at the inclusion step. So the paper's wording describes the search but omits the English-only inclusion criterion. The consequence is unchanged.
Confirmed: F(1, 601) = 2.93 gives P = .087; F(4, 601) = 2.93 gives P = .020 (recomputed).

Confirmed as printed: ref 13 is Eur Neuropsychopharm 2019;29(Suppl 3):S804 with a 2017 DOI (10.1016/j.euroneuro.2017.08.043). It is in the bias-free list and among the 20 new studies. The registration excludes meeting abstracts.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, critically low. Item 4 fails in effect: the 87 carried-over studies come from an English-only search, the registration requires English, and the search window starting 1 July 2016 is unexplained. Item 7 fails: there is no list of excluded studies. Item 2 'partial yes' is generous, since the registration post-dates the stated start of analysis and admits the main patterns were known. It is a critical item either way and does not change the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. Key Points 'Meaning' states no association with protection, but the fully adjusted interval runs to 0.85. The abstract's female estimate uses the any-drinker row, which includes former drinkers (checked: 226 estimates = 204 current + 22 former). The Discussion's 'increased risk from 25 g' does not hold for the pooled estimate or for men. The Figure adds a further point: the non-significance of 0.93 holds only with the whole covariate set.

missed: Figure values (see key finding 6). Taking out almost any single study-level covariate makes the low-volume association significant (0.90 to 0.92, P = .005 to .04). The paper's null depends on including all of them, which the abstract and Key Points do not convey.
The Methods text gives the categories as 1.3-24.0, 25.0-44.0 and 45.0-64.0 g a day, leaving gaps between them. The tables use 1.30 to <25, 25 to <45 and 45 to <65. The abstract uses 1.3-24.0.

The registration also planned analyses 'just on the new studies'. Apart from an unadjusted forest plot of the 20 new studies (eFigure 3, not read), these are not reported. This should be added to the card's list of registered but unreported analyses.

Coders: the registration names two independent coders in its blinding section and three investigators (TS, JZ, SC) for extraction. The paper names three coders (J. Z., F. A., J. C.). The change is not noted.

Publication years of the included studies, from the reference list: the earliest are from 1981 (refs 79, 110, 122). The latest appeared in 2021, two of them in 2022 print issues (refs 30, 31). The search window was January 1980 to July 2021.
